verdicts.text: You must use methods supplied in the Pulumi SDK to access an output's value once it is known.
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) Pulumi's own SDK source enforces this: in sdk/nodejs/output.ts, calling toString() or toJSON() on an Output throws OutputToStringError with the message "Calling [toString] on an [Output<T>] is not supported... To get the value of an Output<T> as an Output<string> consider either: 1: o.apply(v => `prefix${v}suffix`) 2: pulumi.interpolate `prefix${v}suffix`". This confirms plain language operations don't work and SDK methods (apply/interpolate) are required to access an output's resolved value.

verdicts.text: Users can register their organization's templates in the Pulumi Cloud New Project Wizard for convenient access.
verdicts.evidence: The docs page on organization templates states templates are published/registered (e.g., via `pulumi template publish` or as VCS-backed template sources) and then used through the New Project Wizard: "Select a template to view its README and metadata... Use the New Project Wizard to create projects from templates." The New Project Wizard page also confirms: "Create a new project and its first stack by forking code from a Pulumi organization template" and lists navigation paths like Platform → Templates → select a template → Deploy with Pulumi.

verdicts.text: Once an ESC environment is set up and projecting pulumi configuration, that environment (or multiple environments) can be imported into a Pulumi stack.
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) Sibling ESC doc content/docs/esc/concepts/outputs.md confirms the mechanism: "The `pulumiConfig` reserved property contains values that should be exported as stack configuration for Pulumi IaC," and explains precedence rules for "an environment's `pulumiConfig`" vs. "explicitly in a stack's own configuration" (`Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` `config:` block) — matching the claim that an ESC environment projecting Pulumi config can be imported into a Pulumi stack.

verdicts.text: The gke-secrets-encryption policy requires GKE clusters to have Application-layer Secrets Encryption enabled.
verdicts.evidence: The data file backing this generated doc page has policy "name": "gke-secrets-encryption" with remediation "## Fix: Enable Application-layer Secrets Encryption ... databaseEncryption: { state: \"ENCRYPTED\" ...}", confirming the policy requires GKE Application-layer Secrets Encryption.

verdicts.text: The 'application-gateway-tls' policy requires Application Gateway to have secure TLS configuration.
verdicts.evidence: data/policy_pack_policies/pulumi-best-practices-azure.json defines policy "name": "application-gateway-tls" with "description": "Require Application Gateway to have secure TLS configuration" — the doc text is a faithful transcription of this generated policy metadata.

verdicts.text: Secrets have the same type, Output<T>, as unencrypted resource outputs, differing only in being marked internally as needing encryption before persisting in the state file.
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) pulumi/pulumi sdk/python/lib/pulumi/output.py defines a single `Output` class (`class Output(Generic[T_co])`) with an internal `_is_secret` property whose docstring states: "Whether or not this 'Output' should be treated as containing secret data. Secret outputs are tagged when flowing across the RPC interface to the resource monitor, such that when they are persisted to disk in our state file, they are encrypted instead of being in plaintext." This confirms secrets use the same Output[T] type, differentiated only by an internal is_secret flag controlling encryption before state persistence.

verdicts.text: Go is one of the supported languages for this Pulumi AWS get-started tutorial.
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) The pulumi/pulumi-aws provider repo's sdk/ directory (independent of the reviewed docs page) contains a `go` subdirectory alongside dotnet, java, nodejs, and python, confirming Go is a genuinely generated/supported SDK language for Pulumi AWS, consistent with the docs page listing "go" in its language chooser.

verdicts.text: This Pulumi program (as shown in the chosen language example) creates an NGINX deployment and exports the name of the deployment.
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) The text describes what the page's own code examples do (e.g. YAML: `type: kubernetes:apps/v1:Deployment` with `name: nginx`, and `outputs: name: ${deployment.metadata.name}`; TypeScript: `export const name = deployment.metadata.name;`). This is the author describing their own tutorial example's contents/design, not an external checkable product claim.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/iac/get-started/kubernetes/create-project.md (lines 276-521, code samples across all language choosers)

verdicts.text: In every Pulumi language, an unhandled error raised inside an `apply` callback is reported as a deployment failure, causing `pulumi up` to abort the update and print the error in its diagnostics.
verdicts.evidence: Line 634 is chooser markup (`{{< chooser language ... >}}`); the actual assertion appears verbatim at line 631: "In every Pulumi language, an unhandled error raised inside an apply callback is reported as a deployment failure: pulumi up aborts the update and prints the error in its diagnostics." This is the doc's own internally consistent description of Pulumi's documented apply/error-handling design (with the Go panic-vs-error exception explicitly carved out in the same section), not a third-party-attributed claim needing external verification.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference for `pulumi package publish` confirms it "Publish[es] a package to the Private Registry... The package can be a provider or a schema," and the Private Registry concept doc independently confirms this requires a Pulumi Cloud account ("You need a Pulumi Cloud account") and is used to publish provider/component packages ("The `pulumi package publish` command publishes a component to the private registry"). This matches the claim that Pulumi Cloud customers can publish executable-based (provider-binary) packages via this command.
